user: Bond ETFs vs actual bonds
assistant: Bond ETFs and actual bonds differ in several ways. Bond ETFs are traded like normal stock on exchanges such as Nasdaq and the NYSE, while actual bonds are traded over-the-counter (OTC) or directly between two parties. Bond ETFs typically own many bonds and have them laddered so that they are constantly maturing, whereas actual bonds have a fixed maturity date. The value of both bond ETFs and actual bonds is influenced by factors like supply/demand, interest rates, credit ratings, and news. However, with bond ETFs, you're able to lose money as well as gain depending on the situation with the bond market, even if the issuer of the bond does not default. In contrast, when holding an individual bond, your potential loss is limited to the principal amount if the issuer defaults, but you will still receive the periodic interest payments until maturity or default.

user: So, it is more stable because it is diversified than individual bond.  what is a risk factor then?
assistant: Yes, bond ETFs can be considered more stable due to their diversified nature compared to individual bonds. However, a significant risk factor for bond ETFs is interest rate risk. When interest rates rise, the prices of existing bonds typically fall, causing the value of the bond ETF to decrease. Additionally, the international bond ETFs can add 30-100bps of fees, fairly high, over their domestic versions.  Also, bond ETFs may experience tracking error risk, where the performance of the ETF slightly deviates from the performance of the underlying bonds due to management fees, operational costs, and other factors.  it is not uncommon to see the VIX up ~30% with levered ETFs only netting ~10-12% as opposed to the intended 60 or 90%, for example.
[The End of Previous Conversation]

[The Start of Current Turn Question]
What are those abbreviations bps and VIX?  And tell me today's VIX at NASDAQ.
[The End of Current Turn Question]

[The Start of Reference Answer]
BPS stands for "basis points," which are units used to express the percentage change in a financial instrument or investment. One basis point is equal to 0.01% (1 bps is 0.0001) .
VIX  is based on the volatility of the market, using ""market expectation of near term volatility conveyed by stock index option prices" and tracks volatility of the premium of S&P 500 options which become more expensive when traders want to hedge against volatility. It is often referred to as the "fear gauge" because it reflects investors' expectations of market volatility.
As for the current VIX value, I cannot provide real-time data, so I recommend checking a reliable financial news platform.
[The End of Reference Answer]

If you are worried about an increase in volatility, then go long volatility. Volatility itself can be traded. Here in the US there is an index VIX that is described as tracking volatility. What VIX actually tracks is the premium of S&P 500 options, which become more expensive when traders want to hedge against volatility. In the US you can trade VIX options or invest in VIX tracking ETFs like VXX. Apparently there are similar ETFs listed in Canada, such as HUV. Volatility itself is quite volatile so it is possible that a small volatility long position would cover the losses of a larger long position in stocks. If you do choose to invest in a volatility ETF, be aware that they experience quite a lot of decay. You will not want to hold it for very long.

"There is no good proxy for VIX, because it is a completely made-up value. Most listed options trade on an underlying security.  I can therefore choose to buy either the stock, or a future or option on that stock.  In this way, the future and option are derivatives in that they derive their value (in part) based on something else, in this case the stock price as of now. VIX is a different entity altogether.  It is based on the volatility of the market, using ""market expectation of near term volatility conveyed by stock index option prices"".  But the FAQ goes on to state that they are adding factors into the formula. So right away there is no one equity/stock that you can hold that will necessarily match the VIX in any significant way, because it is not directly based on stocks, but indirectly through other options and computations. In effect, therefore, the VIX in indeed only available through its options, and is not observable (tradable) in and of itself."
